rv.q: I have rarely seen actors change from within so subtly and definitively.
Mike Bartlett’s intricately entertaining latest also foregrounds thoughts on how we might be tempted to escape the conformism of everyday coupledom...
Unicorn is pretty sexy by West End standards, exercises the brain as well as other organs and features beguiling performances from its three stars.
It’s a neat idea, but for all its colourful sexual candour (and it is very colourfully candid), Bartlett’s writing is also frustratingly tricksy, repetitive and evasive.
Bartlett writes bitter well — bitterly funny even better. There are some great one-liners and a standout riff by Walker about the joys of “waiting” in the days before mobile phones.
It’s tartly amusing, but also cliche bound.
However intimate the conversation becomes, the chemistry in this throuple never quite ignites.
But for a drama that is concerned with desire, it’s verbose and oddly passionless, and its circuitous musings verge on frustrating.
After the twelfth box of vibrators starts buzzing away, a certain boredom sets in.
Here, the end result is a linguistic joy and a poignant study from every delightfully excruciating angle.
Three’s company in Mike Bartlett’s gloriously funny and deeply empathetic new comedy.
It’s never dull and often devastating, but somehow it fails to land with the weight for which it is striving.

For the most part, Unicorn is lightweight froth but as jealousies and cancer scares emerge, Bartlett firmly places his story in the here-and-now to make a scathing attack on the recent Tory Government.
Like the staging, this production feels empty.
What remains is a safe evening for safe West End audiences.
Unicorn eventually becomes less about the state of the relationship, and more of a state of the nation play.
You can only just accept this as the story coming together neatly, as opposed to it being cheap, easy writing.
So it is a real shame that these ideas feel somewhat half-baked, showing sparks but never quite lighting the fire needed to bring this story to life.

We perhaps knew even earlier that this was dynamite material from a writer at the very top of his game and brought to vivid life by a cast capable of dropping devastating word bombs left, right and centre throughout.

cn.t: Mike Bartlett's throuple comedy boasts a stellar cast (Walker, Mangan, Doherty) but divides critics: some praise its wit and empathy, while others find it overlong, passionless, and more talk than substance.
